item.title: Timing Can Make or Break Culture Change
item.description:
Leadership

Timing Can Make or Break Culture Change

Successful transformation depends not only on what you change, but when.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Timing matters because it can foster or impede the social and psychological conditions that support change.
  • Extrinsic events—like crises, transitions, societal shifts, and tipping points—can help or hinder change.
  • Savvy changemakers pay attention to the broader context and adapt their strategies accordingly.
Source: Maria Di Lorenzo / Unsplash

We often hear that timing is everything when it comes to change. The right moment can open a door; the wrong one can slam it shut. But what does it mean to say that timing matters? Is timing simply beyond our control—or can savvy changemakers use it to their advantage?

Trevor Noah recently discussed the power of timing with former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick, who published a new memoir called The Perilous Fight. Noah reflected on the backlash Kaepernick faced when he protested fatal police shootings of unarmed Black Americans in 2016, by first sitting and then kneeling during the national anthem:

“You were almost, like, ahead of the curve… The timing of when you were doing it made it so that you didn’t have the cover of the collective… You were the one who sticks your head up first.”

Kaepernick sought to inspire change by calling attention to racial disparities in how police use force. At the time, he faced intense scrutiny from both the National Football League (NFL) and segments of the public, which essentially derailed his football career. Yet less than four years later, the issues Kaepernick hoped to advance moved to the center of a nationwide conversation about race and systemic inequality. As Noah points out, Kaepernick’s actions were “ahead of the curve.” What can his experience teach us about why timing matters?

What contextual factors help or hinder culture change?

Situations like the one Kaepernick faced illustrate why the final principle in the intentional culture change framework we’ve been exploring in this series, principle number seven, is that timing matters. Timing matters because it can either foster or impede the social and psychological conditions that support change. Kaepernick acted when he felt the time was right, but the wider culture was resistant—and he paid a significant price.

Many kinds of contextual factors can either block or bolster efforts to change culture. "Never waste a good crisis” is a truism in business and politics. Research shows that crises (like the COVID-19 pandemic), transitions (like changes in leadership), and societal shifts (such as declining institutional trust) can create opportunities for change or reinforce resistance. So, too, can tipping points, like the rapid adoption of generative AI, and major events, like natural disasters. Of course, some of these factors are more predictable than others. But just because they’re difficult to predict doesn’t mean we can’t strategize and prepare.

On the plus side, timing can create openings to design and implement new policies or increase public support for change. One way this happens is when a series of “favorable” conditions align across the culture cycle. For instance, in recent years, public support for greater police accountability, the availability of new technologies, and government funding (at the individual, interaction, and institution levels) helped make police body-worn cameras widespread. Around 80 percent of law enforcement agencies nationwide now use them.

The Culture Cycle
Source: MarYam Hamedani

While openings can widen, they can also narrow again. Consider Kaepernick’s case. Less than four years after his protest began, the viral video of George Floyd’s death, years of organizing around other high-profile police killings, and the unusual conditions created by pandemic lockdowns helped generate unprecedented public attention and participation. The resulting nationwide protests, amplified through social and traditional media, contributed to increased public support for police reform. Yet support for these changes did not endure. Within a few years, a backlash emerged among politicians, policymakers, and communities across the country, leading to an expansion of police budgets, rollbacks of reforms and restrictions, and reduced oversight.

Timing, at its best, provides openings to change attitudes, behaviors, and policies—through shifts in perceived norms, identities, emotions, beliefs about what is possible, and individual and collective efficacy. These social psychological processes can help spread new ideas and behaviors and mobilize collective action.

Pay attention to the broader context—and adapt accordingly

Whether the surrounding conditions are helpful or harmful, savvy changemakers pay attention to the broader context and adapt their approaches accordingly. When mapping out a culture change strategy, ask: What contextual factors may help or hinder culture change? While you can’t anticipate everything, you can develop a nimble mindset and build adaptability into your approach.

Changemakers can also use a variety of psychologically smart strategies to prepare stakeholders for change. For instance, leaders can foster a shared sense that change is possible and needed—or at least unavoidable—and can produce positive outcomes. They can communicate a clear vision of where the changes are headed and ensure that their messages reach key audiences. They can also frame change efforts positively rather than negatively—for example, promoting the benefits of electric vehicles (“quiet is power”) rather than emphasizing the drawbacks of gas-powered cars (“ditch the fumes”).

The right conditions can build momentum for culture change, but these conditions often don’t arise on their own. Changemakers can’t control when the broader culture will be ready, but they can help build that readiness—and they can use “accidents” of good timing to advance the change they seek. Those who seem “ahead of the curve,” like Kaepernick, may also be helping to bend it. So ask yourself: What can I do and when should I do it? And what am I willing to risk?

Intentional Culture Change: 7 Key Principles
Source: MarYam Hamedani

item.title: Don’t Let Small Mistakes Become Big Ones
item.description:
Decision-Making

Don’t Let Small Mistakes Become Big Ones

The decisions we make after a mistake can matter more than the error itself.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Cognitive biases can lead us to turn small mistakes into bigger ones.
  • Recognizing our mistakes requires questioning assumptions we take for granted.
  • Cognitive flexibility helps us change course before small mistakes become bigger problems.

Sometimes, the biggest mistake we can make is refusing to admit that we’ve made one. What could have been a minor misstep then becomes a much bigger problem, not because of what we initially did, but because of what we decided to do—or not do—next. One skill I try to teach, and hone for myself, is cognitive flexibility: When things aren’t working, look for other options. Even so, I’ve turned small mistakes into much bigger ones by not admitting them quickly enough. I’ve also felt the regret of knowing I should have owned my mistake sooner, all while letting the problem become more entrenched and making the hole I had to climb out of deeper.

Cognitive flexibility after a mistake starts with recognizing that each moment is a new decision point. We don’t have to wait for consequences to unfold, double down on bad decisions, or simply hope that somehow things will work out. We can admit what went wrong and change course. Two cognitive biases, however, can stand in the way and turn small mistakes into much bigger ones.

Sunk Cost Fallacy

The sunk cost fallacy concerns the weight we give to what has already happened when deciding what to do next. In financial terms, this is the classic example of “throwing good money after bad,” such as when someone initially invests in a stock and, while watching its value fall, decides not to sell, holding onto hope that they might recover what they have already lost. Of course, it may be wise to keep investing in a falling stock, but it is never a good idea to do so based simply on the hope of a different outcome.

This fallacy also influences our moral decisions. Imagine sharing an unflattering story about a friend or coworker. Halfway through your story, you realize you probably shouldn’t be telling it. Yet, instead of stopping, you think, “I’ve already said this much. There’s no point in stopping now. Maybe if I end with something nice, it won’t seem so bad.” Continuing the story doesn’t undo the harm already done, regardless of how you end it. It simply creates an opportunity to make things worse.

The underlying problem with the sunk cost fallacy is that our thinking becomes rigid. We don’t see other options. In these moments, it helps to remember that past decisions set the context for our next move, but they do not need to determine its direction. Instead, we can recognize our mistake and begin to limit the harm or repair the damage.

Escalation of Commitment

Escalation of commitment occurs when people double down on a failing course of action. For example, consider someone who tells a small white lie. When questioned, rather than admit the truth, they tell a bigger lie to protect the first one. What began as a minor wrongdoing becomes something much more serious through what the person does next.

Sometimes we fall into escalation of commitment because we hope we can turn things around, but other times we do so because admitting our mistake would threaten our self-image. When self-image is a motivating factor, each decision makes it increasingly difficult and costly to admit wrongdoing.

When we fall into either of these cognitive biases, however, our desire to avoid recognizing our mistake prevents us from doing the very thing that could make the consequences, whether to the outcome or to our self-image, less harmful.

Catching Ourselves in the Moment

Before we can correct a mistake, we must first recognize that we’ve made one. Yet often it is extremely difficult to catch ourselves in the act. As Kathryn Schulz, author of Being Wrong, explains in her 2011 TED Talk, “It does feel like something to be wrong; it feels like being right.” It is only when things don’t go as planned that we then become aware of our “error blindness” and experience the embarrassment, discomfort, or anxiety that comes with realizing that we were wrong.

There is, however, another option rather than waiting until a mistake reveals itself to us. Instead of making decisions with blind confidence or constant worry, we can learn to become more aware of what influences our judgment, question the assumptions we take for granted, and seek out information we may be overlooking. In moments when our choices don’t seem to be serving us, we can ask ourselves, “What am I assuming? What might I be missing? What would I do differently if I didn’t already commit to this decision?”

Here, it is important to realize that when it comes to decision-making, practice doesn’t make perfect; it makes room to notice what else is going on around you.

We often assume that we need to be certain we’re wrong before changing course. After all, we tend to believe we’re right until proven otherwise. Yet, by being open to the possibility that our judgments or expectations may be mistaken, we can be more flexible and even more creative in how we respond to unanticipated situations.

Becoming better decision-makers does not mean reaching a point where we no longer make mistakes. It means being more attentive to the possibility that things are not going as planned and being willing to change our course so that small mistakes don’t become much bigger ones.

item.title: A New Database Outs Clergy With Sexual Abuse Allegations
item.description:
Sexual Abuse

A New Database Outs Clergy With Sexual Abuse Allegations

Institutional transparency offers safety to churches and healing to survivors.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Guilty clergy may misrepresent accountability as a "spiritual attack" or rebellion against God's will.
  • Believing that clergy have divine or absolute authority can reduce the likelihood of “upward dissent.”
  • Many churches lack close oversight, misconduct reporting systems, or protocols for external investigations.
  • A new searchable archive allows churches to use its records for hiring screenings.
Source: Thirdman / Pexels

Protestant Accountability contains public records documenting over 2,700 church workers who either committed sexual abuse or mishandled related investigations while holding institutional authority. The database covers church staff broadly, from associate pastors and worship leaders to youth workers and staff who have never preached.

The volunteer-run database accepts entries such as court records, state attorney general reports, news articles, and—since convicted or ousted clergy may switch denominations—data from other survivor-run archives like Stop Baptist Predators, Bishop Accountability, and Survivors Network of Those Abused by Priests (SNAP).

To avoid inviting libel suits, convicted sex offenders are denoted differently than those named in media coverage about pending investigations, charges, or trials. Moreover, the database pulls from credible sources in the public domain, is not investigative, and does not directly influence legal cases, although it can aid law enforcement.

Rather than instigating hearsay or innuendo, the database preserves public documents that broken links and expired pages often erase. This streamlined, searchable archive serves an important purpose: churches can use its records for hiring screenings since Protestant churches have no centralized authority that keeps personnel files.

Founders of Protestant Accountability announced its launch in August at an online press conference organized by the Survivors Network of Those Abused by Priests (SNAP).

Source: John Price / Unsplash

Chellee Taylor, key architect of the database, is a survivor of sexual abuse who in 2022 won a settlement from the Southern Baptist Convention after alleging the denomination covered up her assault at Journey Church in Orange City, Florida.

“I don’t want to burn down the church, but I don’t have a problem dismantling the aspects that are harming people,” Taylor told Christian Today. “The reason that we built this site is because I love the church and I love what the church can and should be. But what it is currently does not mirror that at all.”

Why Survivors Need This

Communities often disbelieve or victim-blame sexual assault survivors, typically placing the burden of proof on survivors and/or subjecting survivors to purity tests before taking their victimization seriously. In fact, multiple studies show that anticipated discrediting is a common reason why approximately 80 percent of survivors do not report sexual assaults.

Source: Josh Applegate / Unsplash

Such swift and pervasive dismissal can saddle survivors with disenfranchised pain, defined as emotional or physical suffering that society does not openly acknowledge, validate, or support. In turn, invalidation can cause a shocking or traumatic experience to feel doubly painful because of abandonment or alienation.

Protestant Accountability’s database validates survivors, even if churches isolate and silence them. That acknowledgment can be life-saving, considering that universality—or mutual validation of shared experience—can catalyze healing.

While collective denial and institutional coverups are not unique to churches—prisons, sports teams, workplaces, and universities mishandle allegations, too—research indicates that certain doctrine can foster authoritarian submission and groupthink that greatly decrease the odds of congregants believing survivors and challenging pastors.

For example, one study found that church members who perceived church leadership as having divine authority were less likely to engage in “upward dissent,” valid and justified disagreement directed toward people higher in a church’s leadership hierarchy.

Relatedly, another study found that clergy can suppress dissent differently than leaders of ordinary organizations. By misconstruing disagreement as sinful opposition to God’s will, pastors are able to conflate their own will with God’s will, and play God themselves.

Institutionally, investigations and research suggest that many Protestant institutions not only lack misconduct reporting mechanisms, but they also lack upstream feedback channels. Constructive criticism usually flows top-down only. Thus, critiquing leaders may seem unfathomable because a model or protocol for dissent is often non-existent.

Source: Karl Fredericks / Unsplash

Systemically, denominational oversight is also limited, given that most Protestant churches have a decentralized and localized governance structure. Research shows that all Protestant churches lack a single universal ecclesiastical hierarchy, even if some congregations are connected to regional bodies or denominations.

This means that pastors can disband disciplinary boards or HR systems if they see fit, conveniently obstructing justice for survivors by undermining accountability processes.

A lack of institutional oversight can also mean that there is no ethical code for practitioners who hold a position of authority over anyone they’re counseling or mentoring. Since there is no uniform standard of pastoral care across Protestantism, many leaders get away with rationalizing pastoral malpractice or religious abuse.

Sexual Trauma Can Fuel Religious Trauma

Survivors of sex abuse within churches often suffer from a specific form of post-traumatic stress syndrome known as religious trauma syndrome. While defining and unpacking the symptomatology is beyond the scope of this post, you can read more about the disorder in my previous posts. What is important to remember is that religious trauma is not simply about the struggle to unlearn harmful dogma and fill a void. It also involves immense grief in the aftermath of losing an entire community and social support system—not to mention grappling with identity erasure, systemic gaslighting, and severe fear of venturing into a world that has been stigmatized as wholly dangerous.

If you or someone you know is a survivor of church-based sex abuse or religious trauma syndrome, reach out to a mental health professional who specializes in these particular sub-areas of trauma recovery. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
